steps.description: The `Sets` library implements a lightweight set of addresses that supports constant-time add, remove, and membership checks. We will look at the internal data layout, then walk through the three core helpers (`add`, `remove`, `contains`) and finally see how another contract (`Whitelist`) relies on them.

The `AddressSet` struct keeps two parallel data-structures:
- `values` (line 10) – a packed array storing every address that belongs to the set.
- `indexes` (line 11) – a mapping from an address to its position *plus one* inside `values`.
Storing `index+1` instead of the raw index means the default value `0` cleanly signals "not present".

`add` keeps insertion O(1) while preventing duplicates:
1. Line 21 calls `contains` – if an index already exists the function bails out (line 22) and returns `false`.
2. Otherwise the address is appended to `values` (line 24).
3. Line 25 stores `self.values.length`, i.e. **index+1**, into `indexes`.  Because Solidity arrays grow after the push, this equals the element’s new position plus one.
Returning `true` confirms the element was newly added.

`remove` performs constant-time deletion via the classic swap-and-pop technique:
1. Fetch the stored index (line 36).  If it is `0`, the value was never inside the set (line 37-39).
2. Subtract one (line 42) to obtain the real array index.
3. Grab the last element’s index (`lastIndex`, line 44).  If the element to delete is *not* the last one (line 46) it:
   - Copies the last element over the soon-to-be-vacant slot (lines 47-48).
   - Updates that element’s `indexes` entry to its new position (`index+1`, line 49).
4. `pop()` (line 52) discards the duplicated tail element.
5. Finally the mapping slot for the removed address is cleared (line 54) and the function returns `true`.

`contains` is just `return indexes[value] != 0;` (line 66).  Because every stored index is shifted by +1, a zero value unambiguously means the address is **not** part of the set.  This single storage read gives an O(1) membership check.
Contracts link the library with `using Sets for Sets.AddressSet` (line 11) and embed a set instance (line 13).

Here is how the `Whitelist` contract leverages the helpers we explored:
- `addresses.add(caller);` (line 31) – adds an account while automatically skipping duplicates.
- `addresses.remove(caller);` (line 41) – removes an account with the swap-and-pop logic.
- `addresses.contains(account);` (line 54) – quick membership check when evaluating `isWhitelisted`.
Thanks to Sets, each operation costs only O(1) storage reads/writes without implementing the data-structure again.
